keyVerseText: Be it known now unto the king, that, if this city be builded, and the walls set up again, then will they not pay toll, tribute, and custom, and so thou shalt endamage the revenue of the kings. pay: Chal. give revenue: or, strength
rootMeaning: The root word מִדָּה (middâh, H4060) primarily conveys the idea of measurement, encompassing dimensions such as height, breadth, or size. This foundation of 'measuring' extends metaphorically to portions or allotments, which naturally includes garments and tribute. The specific form מִנְדָּה (middâh, H4061) derives from an Aramaic loan and retains this concept of a measured portion, here applied to tolls or tributes. Thus, the literal sense emphasizes a fixed, assessed quantity rather than a vague payment, highlighting the regulated and accounted nature of the tribute.
usageInScripture: The term מִנְדָּה appears four times in Scripture, consistently referring to a form of tribute or toll. Its translations—primarily 'toll' and 'tribute'—reflect a narrow semantic range focused on financial or tax obligations. This consistency suggests the word was understood as a specific, recognized payment imposed by authority, rather than a general offering or gift. The limited occurrences reinforce its specialized usage in contexts involving fiscal duties to a governing power.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מִנְדָּה as a measured tribute deepens our grasp of biblical justice and governance, where obligations to earthly authorities are defined and regulated. It reminds believers that earthly authorities have God-ordained roles to collect dues, reflecting order and accountability in society. This measured tribute also points forward to Christ’s fulfillment of all righteous demands, including those of law and justice. Recognizing the precise nature of such tributes underscores the biblical call to honesty and integrity in all transactions, honoring God through faithful stewardship.
keyVerseReflection: Ezra 4:13 states, 'Be it known now unto the king, that, if this city be builded, and the walls set up again, then will they not pay toll, tribute, and custom.' Here, מִנְדָּה underscores the concrete financial obligations that would be forfeited if the city’s reconstruction proceeded. The word highlights the tangible loss of revenue that the king would suffer, emphasizing the economic implications tied to political and spiritual restoration. This verse reminds us that even in matters of faith and rebuilding, earthly responsibilities and their consequences remain significant.
